title: Gandhi and King read him
hookLine: Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr. both drew on this essay

lines: THIS ONE GOT ON A SHIP.
cards: Some sentences stay home, read once in the town they were written in, then asleep on a shelf. Others get on ships.
Thoreau's essay was written by a man who spent one night in a small-town jail and went berry picking the next morning. It's short, prickly, and argues with its own readers.
And yet it turned up, years later, in the hands of a lawyer organizing Indians in South Africa, and later still in the memory of a pastor in Montgomery, Alabama.

teach.b: First, Gandhi. In South Africa, Gandhi was leading Indians in refusing unjust laws when he came across Thoreau's essay. He later wrote that the resistance was already well under way before he read it.
He borrowed Thoreau's phrase, civil disobedience, to explain the struggle to English readers, then found even that phrase didn't carry the whole meaning. Second, Gandhi's own word.

He tells how the movement got its name: satyagraha, which he explained as holding firmly to truth, a force born of truth and love. So the essay was a companion on that road, not its starting point. Third, King.

Martin Luther King Jr. wrote that he first read the essay as a student, fascinated by the idea of refusing to cooperate with an evil system. As a pastor in Montgomery, during the bus boycott, he remembered it.
What the boycotters were saying, he wrote, came down to this: we can no longer lend our cooperation to an evil system. Thoreau's counter friction, carried onto a city bus.
Fourth, each reader changed it. King wrote that the movement's spirit came from Jesus's teaching of love, and its method from Gandhi. Gandhi grounded his in truth; Thoreau grounded his in conscience.
Three people, three sources, one idea of open, peaceful refusal, passed hand to hand. It traveled, and it didn't arrive unchanged.

how: Thoreau's essay is often read alongside Gandhi's and King's own writings, as one voice in a longer conversation about open, nonviolent refusal to cooperate with injustice.

games.q: what does “gandhi and king read him” mean?
o: both men met Thoreau and studied with him in Concord
both drew on Thoreau's essay, each in his own way
both said the essay gave them their whole movement

games.q: who did what with the essay: tap the pairs.
p: borrowed the phrase for English readers
no cooperation with an evil system
a counter friction to stop the machine

s: Gandhi wrote that his movement began because he read Thoreau
he wrote that the resistance in South Africa was well under way before he read the essay.
King wrote that he remembered the essay during the Montgomery bus boycott
the boycott, he wrote, was refusing to lend cooperation to an evil system.
King said the movement's spirit came from Thoreau alone
he named Jesus's teaching of love as its spirit, and Gandhi for its method.

games.q: you're Gandhi. you've borrowed Thoreau's phrase civil disobedience to explain your struggle, but it doesn't say everything. what do you do?
o: keep the phrase and stop explaining.
give the movement a name of its own: satyagraha.
games.why: Gandhi explained satyagraha as holding firmly to truth, a force born of truth and love.

practice: Here is one line from the essay: let your life be a counter friction to stop the machine. Say it once, slowly, and notice which word catches, life, friction or machine; you don't have to agree with it.
If it stirs a name, someone who once refused something for the right reason, hold them in mind too.

wordCard.voice: Gandhi and King read him. Thoreau's essay reached South Africa and Montgomery, and each reader made it their own. Today's word.

orig.note: satyagraha, the name Gandhi gave his movement; he explained it as holding firmly to truth.

carryVoice: Your line: it traveled. A good sentence can cross an ocean and arrive changed. Go gently.
